newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain refuses to budge on wages despite strike.
newsitem.headline: Spain refuses to budge on wages despite strike.

text.p: Spain's conservative government vowed not to budge on its pay freeze despite a strike by civil servants on Wednesday which it said was heeded by only one in five, not four in five as the unions claimed.

Trade unions called out two million civil servants for a 24-hour strike in protest against a freeze on their 1997 salaries, which the government says is vital to meet the criteria to qualify for Europe's single currency.
But the government said only 18 to 20 percent of civil servants had actually heeded the call, in sharp contrast to union estimates of 80 percent support.
While trade union leaders celebrated the strike as a great success, the government dismissed it as a miserable failure and said it would not to be swayed from its 1997 austerity budget.
"(The salary freeze) was not a whimsical decision and defends the interests of Spain in the light of its integration into a monetary union," Administration Minister Mariano Rajoy said in Parliament.
"Civil servants have acted in a responsible way and have clearly understood that the government must adopt various harsh measures including the 1997 salary freeze," he said.
Tens of thousands of workers took to the streets in regional capitals to protest against the wage freeze.
In Barcelona, police said more than 100,000 people had demonstrated, some throwing fish, oranges and eggs at government buildings.

In Madrid, trade unions said around 150,000 people gathered in the city centre, whistling and chanting songs accusing the government of manipulating the turnout figures and calling for a general strike.
Union leaders said they would keep up their fight against the government's tough budget plan and could not rule out the possibility of further strikes.

"If the government maintains its closed and obstinate attitude, refusing to move even an inch, we must warn that we will continue industrial action as long as necessary until the problems are solved," said one union leader.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told Parliament on Wednesday his party was open to talks but reiterated the wage freeze was not negotiable.
The conservative government took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule. It sparked mass protests in July by announcing a freeze on public sector salaries in 1997 in order to trim the budget.

The unions, led by the Workers' Commission (CCOO) and by UGT, say the freeze violates a deal with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise next year in line with inflation.

The Popular Party government made an election promise to push Spain into EMU and says the 1997 freeze is an essential part of its austere draft budget aimed at bringing the deficit down to the level required to join the single currency in 1999.
